title: CPR for an adult: recognising cardiac arrest and getting help
intro: If someone is unresponsive now, call emergency services immediately: 112 in the European Union and Moldova, or the local emergency number elsewhere. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher's instructions. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR. This article explains adult basic life support; children, drowning and other special situations require additional guidance.

sections.heading: Check safety, response and breathing
paragraphs: Make sure you can approach safely, then speak loudly and gently shake the person's shoulders to check for a response. Shout for help and call immediately if they are unresponsive; assess breathing while connecting to the dispatcher. Occasional gasps, slow laboured breaths or abnormal panting do not count as normal breathing. Tell the dispatcher what you see rather than spending time trying to diagnose the cause or find a pulse. If uncertain about abnormal breathing, let the dispatcher help you recognise cardiac arrest.

sections.heading: Start chest compressions
paragraphs: For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, begin compressions promptly. Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest on the lower half of the breastbone, the other hand on top, and interlock the fingers. Keep arms straight and shoulders above the chest. Press at 100–120 compressions per minute, to a depth of at least 5 cm but no more than 6 cm. Let the chest return fully after each compression, avoiding leaning on it. Minimise interruptions; follow dispatcher guidance if positioning is difficult.

sections.heading: Rescue breaths depend on training
paragraphs: If trained and able to give rescue breaths, alternate 30 compressions with 2 breaths, using the technique you learned and enough air for the chest to start rising. Avoid excessive ventilation and long pauses. If you are untrained, unable or unwilling to give breaths, provide continuous chest compressions and follow the dispatcher. Do not delay compressions while searching for equipment. Breaths are especially important in some situations such as drowning and in children; tell the dispatcher if either applies rather than assuming the adult instructions cover every emergency.

sections.heading: Use an automated external defibrillator
paragraphs: Ask another person to fetch an automated external defibrillator, or AED, if available, while CPR continues. Switch it on, expose the chest, attach the pads as shown and follow its spoken or visual prompts. Keep everyone clear while it analyses the rhythm and when a shock is delivered. Resume compressions promptly when instructed, including when no shock is advised. The device assesses whether a shock is needed; prior training is not required to follow its prompts. Do not leave ongoing CPR merely to search for a distant device when another helper can retrieve it.

sections.heading: Continue and get support afterwards
paragraphs: Continue until professionals take over, the person clearly shows signs of life and breathes normally, you are physically unable to continue, or the scene becomes unsafe. Occasional gasping alone is not a reason to stop. If normal breathing returns, follow the dispatcher's instructions, watch breathing closely and be ready to restart CPR if it becomes abnormal again. CPR and early defibrillation improve the chance of survival but cannot guarantee recovery. Afterwards, rescuers may need emotional support. Practical training and refreshers help people act confidently in a future emergency.

examples.title: Gasping after collapse — hypothetical example
examples.text: An adult collapses and does not respond but makes occasional gasps. A bystander calls on speaker, describes the breathing and starts compressions with the dispatcher's help rather than assuming the gasps mean normal breathing.

examples.title: Sharing tasks — hypothetical example
examples.text: At a sports venue, one person calls and begins CPR while another retrieves the nearby AED. They follow the device's prompts, keep clear during analysis and shock, and resume compressions when instructed.
